drills.title: The menu loop
drills.prompt: The array typed stands in for what the user types. Arrange the lines into a menu loop that stops at q and then says goodbye. The first two lines can go in either order, and count++ may sit before or after the if. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: while (true) repeats forever, so the loop needs a way out: break inside an if. Inside it the pattern is read, check, act. The choice is a String, so it is compared with equals and a text in double quotes, never with == and a char in single quotes ('q'). The last line sits after the closing brace, so it runs once the loop is over.

drills.title: Withdrawal rules
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program checks the withdrawal of Rs. 300 and prints the goal output.
drills.explain: A withdrawal must be a multiple of 100: amount % 100 is the remainder, and it must be 0. The funds check asks whether the amount is bigger than the balance. The reason is a String, so it is compared with equals, never ==. %,.2f prints a number with a thousands comma and exactly two decimals; %d only accepts whole numbers and would crash on a double.

drills.title: What the menu says
drills.prompt:
The program reads its answers from the keyboard. The user types these five lines (the second one is an x, the third has spaces around the 1, the fourth is a capital Q):

```
1
x
 1 
Q
q
```

Type exactly what the program prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: trim() removes the spaces around the third answer, so it counts as a 1. x matches nothing and goes to else. equals is case-sensitive, so Q is not q: it is also invalid, and the loop only stops at the lower-case q. The program reads every answer with nextLine() and the loop prints nothing for the valid 1s.

drills.title: The right PIN is refused
drills.prompt: The user types the correct PIN 1234, but the ATM says Wrong PIN. The program compiles and runs without error. Click the faulty line and choose the fix.
drills.explain: == asks whether two Strings are the very same object. The text the user typed was built by Scanner, so it is a different object from the literal "1234" even with the same letters. equals compares the letters. A single = is an assignment and does not compile, and equals(1234) compares a text with a number, which is never equal.

drills.title: Review the AI's withdraw loop
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this withdrawal loop for the ATM. It compiles and works for the happy path, but tick the real problems (there are three).

issues.text: A new Scanner is created on every round of the loop
issues.why: Create the Scanner once before the loop. Each new one wraps the same keyboard and can swallow input that an earlier one already buffered.

issues.text: Typing letters such as abc makes Integer.parseInt throw NumberFormatException and the ATM crashes
issues.why: User input is untrusted. Catch the error or check the text before parsing, then ask again.

issues.text: Any amount is accepted: negative numbers add money and amounts above the balance make it negative
issues.why: The ATM rules from the lesson are missing: a positive multiple of 100, not above the balance (and the daily limit). Check them before changing the balance.

non_issues.text: while (true) never ends, so the program hangs
non_issues.why: The break on line 11 leaves the loop when the user types 0. while (true) with a break is the standard menu-loop pattern.

non_issues.text: trim() is pointless here and should be removed
non_issues.why: Integer.parseInt(" 500") fails on spaces, so trimming the typed text first prevents a crash.

non_issues.text: balance must be a double because it is money
non_issues.why: Here the balance holds whole rupees and an int is exact. A double is only needed when there are paise.

drills.explain: Generated console programs often work for one tidy run and fail on the first surprise. Check where the Scanner is created, what happens on bad input, and whether the business rules are really there.
